about: T11 captions, written as a warm tutor speaking; each line starts at film time t (seconds). Can be recorded as voiceover later.

lines.text: Lesson eleven: spot versus futures. What do you really own when you trade?
Asha and Rahul both think BTC might rise. Both trade 0.010 BTC at 60,000.
Asha buys on spot. Rahul opens a long futures position.
If BTC rises, both gain. So what's the difference?
Spot means buying the actual asset, paid in full, and it's yours right away.
Like buying a gold coin at a shop. You pay, and you take the coin home.
Asha pays 600 USDT, and 0.010 BTC lands in her wallet. She owns it.
A futures contract is an agreement about the price of an asset. It is not the asset itself.
The asset it follows is called the underlying. Here, the underlying is BTC.
Rahul opens a long contract for 0.010 BTC. No BTC arrives. He holds a contract.
Most crypto futures are perpetual. A perpetual contract has no end date.
Older-style futures expire on a set date. A perpetual stays open until it's closed.
When it closes, profit or loss is settled in USDT. No coins are delivered.
Exposure is how much of your money moves with the price.
Notional value is the full size of a position: size × price.
0.010 BTC × 60,000 = 600 USDT. Asha and Rahul both have 600 USDT of exposure.
Now let's follow the same price for both, side by side.
BTC rises to 63,000. Asha's coins are worth 630 USDT. Rahul's PnL is +30 USDT.
BTC falls to 57,000. Asha's coins: 570 USDT. Rahul's PnL: −30 USDT.
Same moves, same money. But only Asha owns any BTC.
Futures can also go short: you gain if the price falls, and lose if it rises.
Short 0.010 BTC from 60,000. At 57,000: +30 USDT. At 63,000: −30 USDT.
On plain spot, you can only sell coins you already hold.
A common mistake: thinking a futures position means you own the coin.
You can't withdraw BTC from a futures position. There is no coin to send.
Correction: futures give price exposure. Spot gives ownership.
Futures add risks that plain spot doesn't have.
Margin and leverage: a small deposit controls a bigger position. That's lesson T12.
Liquidation: if losses eat your margin, the exchange can close the position for you.
Funding: perpetual traders pay or receive small amounts at set times. More in T13.
Your turn. Spot or futures? Sort these five. Pause if you need more time.
Holding coins in your wallet, and withdrawing them: spot.
A perpetual long, funding payments and liquidation: all futures.
Well done if you sorted them all!
Here's the whole picture in one table.
With spot, you hold the coin and pay the full price. No expiry, no funding, no liquidation.
With perpetual futures, you hold a contract. You can go long or short.
And you face funding and liquidation.
Neither one is safe. Spot prices can fall a lot, and you can lose money.
Futures can lose faster, and a position can be closed for you.
Fees and funding keep adding up while a futures position stays open.
When unsure, WAIT. NO_TRADE is always allowed.
Spot means you buy and own the actual coin.
Futures are contracts about a price. You can go long or short, but you own no coin.
Futures add funding, leverage and liquidation risk.
Check yourself: you hold a BTC perpetual long. Do you own any BTC?
No. You hold a contract that follows the BTC price.
Great work! Next up, T12: margin and leverage, and why they magnify losses as well as gains.
